runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The board is nearly empty, with only an X at the bottom of column 3 and an O directly above it in the same column. Column 3's vertical line is now blocked for X (an O sits between the two X pieces), so stacking another X there would be suboptimal as it prevents any chance of a vertical win in that column while also handing O a strong central block.

Instead, the strongest continuation is to play adjacent to the existing X at the bottom of an open column. This creates a base for multiple potential lines (horizontal along row 5, plus both diagonals) without immediately allowing O to force a response in the center. Columns 2 and 4 are symmetric and equally strong; column 4 is selected here to begin building rightward threats around the existing central X.

No immediate win or forced block exists yet (only two X pieces total), so this is a pure positional strengthening move consistent with standard Connect 4 opening theory.

Final Answer: 4

action.thoughts:
We have a 6x7 board (rows 0..5 top->bottom). Current occupied cells:
- o at (4,3)
- x at (5,3) and (5,4)

Legal moves are any column whose top (row 0) is empty — all columns are legal here. Available drop rows:
- col0,1,2,5,6 -> row5
- col3 -> row3 (rows 5 and 4 occupied)
- col4 -> row4 (row5 occupied)

Best move is to play the center column 3. Dropping at column 3 places o at (3,3), building a vertical pair (rows 3-4) in the central column and increasing control of the center. This both advances o’s offensive potential (multiple directions to extend to four) and prevents x from freely stacking above the x at (5,3). No immediate opponent 4-in-a-row threat requires an urgent block, so central control is optimal.

Final Answer: 3

action.thoughts:
The current board state has x pieces at the bottom of columns 3 and 4, with o pieces stacked in column 3 (but no immediate threats from o, as they have only two pieces total and cannot complete four-in-a-row on their next turn). 

No move allows x to win immediately (adding one piece to the existing two cannot form a line of four). However, dropping in column 5 places an x at the bottom of column 5. This creates three consecutive x pieces along the bottom row (columns 3-5). 

The open ends on both sides of this line (columns 2 and 6) each represent an immediate winning threat on the next turn, as playing either would extend to four-in-a-row horizontally. o can block at most one of these on their turn and has no winning move available, so x forces a win on the following turn regardless of o's response. 

This is a classic forcing fork and is superior to other options (such as column 2, which is symmetrically equivalent, or moves like column 4, which create no forcing threats). 

Final Answer: 5
